DOCTOR VISIT LESSON · DOCTOR VISIT · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Deep Breath — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the deep breath as a two-part trick: breathe in like smelling a flower, out like blowing a candle — and the doctor hears exactly what she needs.

What is this?

A deep breath is a slow breath in through the nose and a long breath out — the doctor asks for it during the listening part of the check-up.

What does it mean?

A slow out-breath is the body&rsquo;s own calm button. Teaching it for the doctor quietly hands the child a tool for every hard moment after: the dark bedroom, the big feelings, the long wait.

What does the child need to know?

You need the card and imagination. Flower (cup the hands, sniff sniff) then candle (pursed lips, looooong blow). Five rounds is a full game. That is the whole skill.

Why this matters

The doctor listens MORE when the breath is slow and deep — and the child can hear the difference in their own chest. Cooperation here feels like a superpower, because it is one.

What it teaches

Breath control (a real regulation skill), imagination pairing (flower, candle), and the first experience of calming a body on purpose.

Words to learn

deep breathsmellblowflowercandleslow

Say this to your child

“"Deep breath! Breathe in and out slowly. Smell the flower… blow the candle… again! The doctor hears your wind — what a strong, slow breath."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "breathe in and out slowly."
  2. The flower: hands cupped, sniff sniff sniff — breathe in.
  3. The candle: lips small, looooong blow — breathe out. Not too fast, or the candle laughs!
  4. Five rounds, then listen: hand on the chest, "feel the wind?"
  5. At the visit: "flower… candle…" — and the stethoscope gets its best listen.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the words "deep breath — breathe in and out slowly" sit over a doctor listening with a stethoscope while a child sits calmly on the exam bed, teddy bear beside.

Ask your child

"How do we breathe in?" (smell the flower) "How do we breathe out?" (blow the candle) "When does the doctor ask for a deep breath?" (while listening)

What your child can say or do

Your child might flower-and-candle at bedtime unprompted, coach the whole family through five rounds, or blow out every imaginary candle in the house.

Out in the real world

The same trick works at birthday candles, soup that is too hot and big feelings at bedtime — one skill, a thousand candles.

Try it together

Candle Factory: line up ten imaginary candles; blow them out one at a time, slowly, then relight them with a sniff of a flower. The child who can light and blow ten candles owns the calm-down.

Understanding check

Ask: "How do we breathe for the doctor?" (slow — flower in, candle out) "Why slow?" (so the doctor hears the wind) "When else does the trick work?" (any big feeling)

Staying safe

Breathing games are always gentle — no breath-holding contests. In means sniff, out means blow, and dizziness means stop and rest. Say the rule once, keep it.

This lesson pairs with the Deep Breath flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Doctor Visit.
